claim: Trained neural network models that exhibit features of neural activity recorded from behaving animals may provide insights into circuit mechanisms of cognitive functions through systematic analysis of network activity and connectivity.
source: Trained neural network models, which exhibit features of neural activity recorded from behaving animals, may provide insights into the circuit mechanisms of cognitive functions through systematic analysis of network activity and connectivity.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of trained neural network models, presented as a hypothesis or motivation for the work.

claim: Animals learn from reward feedback on definite actions through reinforcement learning, in contrast to graded error signals commonly used in supervised learning.
source: However, in contrast to the graded error signals commonly used to train networks through supervised learning, animals learn from reward feedback on definite actions through reinforcement learning.
evidence: This statement draws on established understanding of animal learning and reinforcement learning principles.

claim: Reward maximization is particularly relevant when optimal behavior depends on an animal's internal judgment of confidence or subjective preferences.
source: Reward maximization is particularly relevant when optimal behavior depends on an animal's internal judgment of confidence or subjective preferences.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about when reward-based learning is most appropriate, based on reasoning about task structure.

claim: The authors implemented reward-based training of recurrent neural networks in which a value network guides learning by using the activity of the decision network to predict future reward.
source: Here, we implement reward-based training of recurrent neural networks in which a value network guides learning by using the activity of the decision network to predict future reward.
evidence: This describes the methodology implemented in the study.

claim: The reward-based trained models capture behavioral and electrophysiological findings from well-known experimental paradigms.
source: We show that such models capture behavioral and electrophysiological findings from well-known experimental paradigms.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the results demonstrated in the paper, supported by the data presented in subsequent figures.

claim: The work provides a unified framework for investigating diverse cognitive and value-based computations.
source: Our work provides a unified framework for investigating diverse cognitive and value-based computations, and predicts a role for value representation that is essential for learning, but not executing, a task.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution and implications of the work.

claim: The work predicts a role for value representation that is essential for learning, but not executing, a task.
source: Our work provides a unified framework for investigating diverse cognitive and value-based computations, and predicts a role for value representation that is essential for learning, but not executing, a task.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model architecture and results.

claim: Model neural networks optimized for visual object recognition can reproduce important features of neural activity recorded in cortical areas of behaving animals.
source: Recent work has shown that model neural networks optimized for a wide range of tasks, including visual object recognition (Cadieu et al., 2014; Yamins et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2016), perceptual decision-making and working memory (Mante et al., 2013; Barak et al., 2013; Carnevale et al., 2015; Song et al., 2016; Miconi, 2016), timing and sequence generation (Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Rajan et al., 2015), and motor reach (Hennequin et al., 2014; Sussillo et al., 2015), can reproduce important features of neural activity recorded in numerous cortical areas of behaving animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Model neural networks optimized for perceptual decision-making and working memory can reproduce important features of neural activity recorded in cortical areas of behaving animals.
source: Recent work has shown that model neural networks optimized for a wide range of tasks, including visual object recognition (Cadieu et al., 2014; Yamins et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2016), perceptual decision-making and working memory (Mante et al., 2013; Barak et al., 2013; Carnevale et al., 2015; Song et al., 2016; Miconi, 2016), timing and sequence generation (Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Rajan et al., 2015), and motor reach (Hennequin et al., 2014; Sussillo et al., 2015), can reproduce important features of neural activity recorded in numerous cortical areas of behaving animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Model neural networks optimized for timing and sequence generation can reproduce important features of neural activity recorded in cortical areas of behaving animals.
source: Recent work has shown that model neural networks optimized for a wide range of tasks, including visual object recognition (Cadieu et al., 2014; Yamins et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2016), perceptual decision-making and working memory (Mante et al., 2013; Barak et al., 2013; Carnevale et al., 2015; Song et al., 2016; Miconi, 2016), timing and sequence generation (Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Rajan et al., 2015), and motor reach (Hennequin et al., 2014; Sussillo et al., 2015), can reproduce important features of neural activity recorded in numerous cortical areas of behaving animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Model neural networks optimized for motor reach can reproduce important features of neural activity recorded in cortical areas of behaving animals.
source: Recent work has shown that model neural networks optimized for a wide range of tasks, including visual object recognition (Cadieu et al., 2014; Yamins et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2016), perceptual decision-making and working memory (Mante et al., 2013; Barak et al., 2013; Carnevale et al., 2015; Song et al., 2016; Miconi, 2016), timing and sequence generation (Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Rajan et al., 2015), and motor reach (Hennequin et al., 2014; Sussillo et al., 2015), can reproduce important features of neural activity recorded in numerous cortical areas of behaving animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous applications of trained RNNs to cognitive-type behavior have focused on supervised learning from graded error signals.
source: Previous applications of this approach to 'cognitive-type' behavior such as perceptual decision-making and working memory have focused on supervised learning from graded error signals.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior work in the field.

claim: In supervised learning, the network is given the correct response on each trial in the form of a continuous target output to be followed.
source: Unlike in supervised learning where the network is given the correct response on each trial in the form of a continuous target output to be followed, reinforcement learning provides evaluative feedback to the network on whether each selected action was 'good' or 'bad.'
evidence: This is a definition/description of supervised learning, which is established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: Reinforcement learning provides evaluative feedback to the network on whether each selected action was 'good' or 'bad.'
source: Unlike in supervised learning where the network is given the correct response on each trial in the form of a continuous target output to be followed, reinforcement learning provides evaluative feedback to the network on whether each selected action was 'good' or 'bad.'
evidence: This is a definition/description of reinforcement learning, which is established knowledge.

claim: In a perceptual decision-making task with postdecision wagering, on a random half of the trials the animal can opt for a sure choice that results in a small but certain reward.
source: In a perceptual decision-making task with postdecision wagering, for example, on a random half of the trials the animal can opt for a sure choice that results in a small (compared to the correct choice) but certain reward (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
evidence: This describes an experimental paradigm from cited work.

claim: The optimal decision regarding whether to select the sure choice depends on the animal's own confidence in its decision during the trial.
source: The optimal decision regarding whether or not to select the sure choice depends not only on the task condition, such as the proportion of coherently moving dots, but also on the animal's own confidence in its decision during the trial.
evidence: This is an inference about the task structure and what determines optimal behavior.

claim: Learning to make confidence-based judgments cannot be reduced to reproducing a predetermined target output without providing the full probabilistic solution to the network.
source: Learning to make this judgment cannot be reduced to reproducing a predetermined target output without providing the full probabilistic solution to the network.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the limitations of supervised learning for certain tasks.

claim: Supervised learning is often not appropriate for value-based decision-making where the 'correct' judgment depends explicitly on rewards associated with different actions.
source: Meanwhile, supervised learning is often not appropriate for value-based, or economic, decision-making where the 'correct' judgment depends explicitly on rewards associated with different actions, even for identical sensory inputs (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).
evidence: This is an argument about the appropriateness of different learning paradigms, referencing a specific experimental context.

claim: Reward plays a central role in all types of animal learning.
source: More fundamentally, reward plays a central role in all types of animal learning (Sugrue et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a general principle about animal learning supported by citation.

claim: The networks consist of two modules in an 'actor-critic' architecture, in which a decision network selects actions that maximize reward while a value network predicts future reward and guides learning.
source: The networks consist of two modules in an 'actor-critic' architecture (Barto et al., 1983; Grondman et al., 2012), in which a decision network uses inputs provided by the environment to select actions that maximize reward, while a value network uses the selected actions and activity of the decision network to predict future reward and guide learning.
evidence: This describes the architecture used in the study, with citations to the actor-critic framework.

claim: The trained network for the simple perceptual decision-making task learns to integrate sensory evidence to make the correct decision about which of two noisy inputs is larger.
source: For the example perceptual decision-making task above, the trained network learns to integrate the sensory evidence to make the correct decision about which of two noisy inputs is larger (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the performance data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Longer stimulus durations allow the network to improve its performance by continuing to integrate the incoming sensory evidence.
source: As with monkeys performing the task, longer stimulus durations allow the network to improve its performance by continuing to integrate the incoming sensory evidence (Wang, 2002; Kiani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison to animal behavior, supported by citations and implied by the data in Figure 1C.

claim: The output of the value network shows that expected reward is modulated by stimulus difficulty.
source: Indeed, the output of the value network shows that the expected reward (in this case equivalent to confidence) is modulated by stimulus difficulty (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Prior to stimulus onset, the expected reward is the same for all trial conditions and approximates the overall reward rate.
source: Prior to the onset of the stimulus, the expected reward is the same for all trial conditions and approximates the overall reward rate; incoming sensory evidence then allows the network to distinguish its chances of success.
evidence: This is an observation about the value network output, visible in Figure 1E.

claim: Individual units in the decision network exhibit coherence-dependent ramping activity when sorted by signed coherence.
source: Sorting the activity of individual units in the network by the signed coherence (the strength of the evidence, with negative values indicating evidence for L and positive for R) also reveals coherence-dependent ramping activity (Figure 1D) as observed in neural recordings from numerous perceptual decision-making experiments, e.g., Roitman and Shadlen (2002).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and compared to experimental findings via citation.

claim: Coherence-dependent ramping activity has been observed in neural recordings from numerous perceptual decision-making experiments.
source: Sorting the activity of individual units in the network by the signed coherence (the strength of the evidence, with negative values indicating evidence for L and positive for R) also reveals coherence-dependent ramping activity (Figure 1D) as observed in neural recordings from numerous perceptual decision-making experiments, e.g., Roitman and Shadlen (2002).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental findings, supported by citation.

claim: Expected return is computed by the value network by performing an 'absolute value'-like operation on the accumulated evidence.
source: This pattern of activity illustrates why a nonlinear readout by the value network is useful: expected return is computed by performing an 'absolute value'-like operation on the accumulated evidence (plus shifts), as illustrated by the overlap of the expected return for positive and negative-coherence trials (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The time at which the network commits to a decision is unambiguously given by the time at which the selected action is L or R.
source: Here, the time at which the network commits to a decision is unambiguously given by the time at which the selected action is L or R.
evidence: This is a statement about how decision time is defined in the model.

claim: The appropriate speed-accuracy tradeoff is learned in the space of concrete actions in reward-based training.
source: Thus the appropriate speed-accuracy tradeoff is learned in the space of concrete actions, illustrating the desirability of using reward-based training of RNNs when modeling reaction-time tasks.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the reward-based approach.

claim: Networks were trained for three well-known behavioral paradigms in which the correct behavior is predetermined on each trial by the task condition alone.
source: In addition to the example task from the previous section, we trained networks for three well-known behavioral paradigms in which the correct, or optimal, behavior is (pre-)determined on each trial by the task condition alone.
evidence: This describes the tasks studied in the paper.

claim: Similar tasks have previously been addressed with several different forms of supervised learning, including FORCE, Hessian-free, and stochastic gradient descent.
source: Similar tasks have previously been addressed with several different forms of supervised learning, including FORCE (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009; Carnevale et al., 2015), Hessian-free (Martens and Sutskever, 2011; Mante et al., 2013; Barak et al., 2013), and stochastic gradient descent (Pascanu et al., 2013b; Song et al., 2016), so that the results shown in Figure 2 are presented as confirmation that the same tasks can also be learned using reward feedback on definite actions alone.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The network successfully learned to perform the context-dependent integration task.
source: The network successfully learned to perform the task, which is reflected in the psychometric functions showing the percentage of trials on which the network chose R as a function of the signed motion and color coherences, where motion and color indicate the two sources of noisy information and the sign is positive for R and negative for L (Figure 2A, left).
evidence: This is supported by the psychometric functions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Units in the decision network show mixed selectivity when sorted by different combinations of task variables in the context-dependent integration task.
source: As in electrophysiological recordings, units in the decision network show mixed selectivity when sorted by different combinations of task variables (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and compared to experimental findings.

claim: The trained network for the multisensory integration task exhibits multisensory enhancement in which performance on multisensory trials was better than on single-modality trials.
source: As shown in the psychometric function (percentage of high choices as a function of event rate, Figure 2B, left), the trained network exhibits multisensory enhancement in which performance on multisensory trials was better than on single-modality trials.
evidence: This is shown in the psychometric function in Figure 2B.

claim: Decision network units in the multisensory integration task exhibit a range of tuning to task parameters, with some selective to choice, others to modality, and many showing mixed selectivity.
source: As observed in electrophysiological recordings, moreover, decision network units exhibit a range of tuning to task parameters, with some selective to choice and others to modality, while many units showed mixed selectivity to all task variables (Figure 2B, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and compared to experimental findings.

claim: RNNs trained with reward feedback alone can reproduce the mixed selectivity characteristic of neural populations in higher cortical areas.
source: Figure 2 and the following make clear, however, that RNNs trained with reward feedback alone can already reproduce the mixed selectivity characteristic of neural populations in higher cortical areas (Rigotti et al., 2010, 2013), thereby providing a valuable platform for future investigations of how such complex representations are learned.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the results, with citations to work on mixed selectivity.

claim: In a postdecision wager task, the optimal decision depends on the animal's estimate of the probability that its decision is correct, i.e., its confidence.
source: In a postdecision wager task (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009), however, the optimal decision depends on the animal's (agent's) estimate of the probability that its decision is correct, i.e., its confidence.
evidence: This is a statement about the task structure, referencing the experimental paradigm.

claim: The network opted for the sure option more frequently when the coherence was low or stimulus duration short.
source: The key behavioral features found in Kiani and Shadlen (2009); Wei and Wang (2015) are reproduced in the trained network, namely the network opted for the sure option more frequently when the coherence was low or stimulus duration short (Figure 3B, left); and when the network was presented with a sure option but waived it in favor of choosing L or R, the performance was better than on trials when the sure option was not presented (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and compared to experimental findings via citations.

claim: When the network was presented with a sure option but waived it in favor of choosing L or R, the performance was better than on trials when the sure option was not presented.
source: The key behavioral features found in Kiani and Shadlen (2009); Wei and Wang (2015) are reproduced in the trained network, namely the network opted for the sure option more frequently when the coherence was low or stimulus duration short (Figure 3B, left); and when the network was presented with a sure option but waived it in favor of choosing L or R, the performance was better than on trials when the sure option was not presented (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and compared to experimental findings via citations.

claim: Neither monkeys nor trained networks choose the sure target on the basis of stimulus difficulty alone but based on their internal sense of uncertainty on each trial.
source: The latter observation is taken as indication that neither monkeys nor trained networks choose the sure target on the basis of stimulus difficulty alone but based on their internal sense of uncertainty on each trial.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: On trials in which the sure option was chosen, the firing rate of decision network units is intermediate compared to trials on which the network made a decision by choosing L or R.
source: In particular, on trials in which the sure option was chosen, the firing rate is intermediate compared to trials on which the network made a decision by choosing L or R.
evidence: This is an observation about neural activity shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the economic choice task, information regarding whether an answer is correct is not contained in the inputs but rather in the association between inputs and rewards.
source: In contrast to the previous tasks, however, information regarding whether an answer is correct in this sense is not contained in the inputs but rather in the association between inputs and rewards.
evidence: This is a statement about the task structure that distinguishes it from cognitive tasks.

claim: No changes were made to the network architecture for the value-based economic choice task.
source: We emphasize that no changes were made to the network architecture for this value-based economic choice task.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology.

claim: The work expands the range of tasks and corresponding neural mechanisms that can be studied by analyzing model recurrent neural networks.
source: Our main contributions are twofold: first, our work expands the range of tasks and corresponding neural mechanisms that can be studied by analyzing model recurrent neural networks, providing a unified setting in which to study diverse computations and compare to electrophysiological recordings from behaving animals
evidence: This is a summary of the contribution of the work.

claim: By explicitly incorporating reward into network training, the work makes it possible to more directly address the question of reward-related processes in the brain.
source: second, by explicitly incorporating reward into network training, our work makes it possible in the future to more directly address the question of reward-related processes in the brain, for instance the role of value representation that is essential for learning, but not executing, a task.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications and future potential of the work.

claim: The specific form of the baseline network inputs used in this work has not been used previously in the context of recurrent policy gradients.
source: To our knowledge, the specific form of the baseline network inputs used in this work has not been used previously in the context of recurrent policy gradients
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach.

claim: For some of the simpler tasks, models with a baseline consisting of a linear readout of the selected actions and decision network activity could be trained in comparable but slightly longer time.
source: Indeed, the latter architecture is quite common in machine learning applications (Mnih et al., 2016), and likewise, for some of the simpler tasks considered here, models with a baseline consisting of a linear readout of the selected actions and decision network activity could be trained in comparable (but slightly longer) time (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: A separate value network to represent the baseline suggests an explicit role for value representation in the brain that is essential for learning a task but not for executing an already learned task.
source: Interestingly, a separate value network to represent the baseline suggests an explicit role for value representation in the brain that is essential for learning a task (equivalently, when the environment is changing), but not for executing an already learned task, as is sometimes found in experiments (Turner and Desmurget, 2010; Schoenbaum et al., 2011; Stalnaker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model architecture in light of experimental findings, supported by citations.

claim: An accurate baseline dramatically improves learning but is not required.
source: Since an accurate baseline dramatically improves learning but is not required—the algorithm is less reliable and takes many samples to converge with a constant baseline, for instance—this baseline network hypothesis for the role of value representation may account for some of the subtle yet broad learning deficits observed in OFC-lesioned animals (Wallis, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the algorithm's behavior and its potential biological implications.

claim: Expected reward is closely related to decision confidence in many of the tasks considered.
source: Moreover, since expected reward is closely related to decision confidence in many of the tasks considered, a value network that nonlinearly reads out confidence information from the decision network is consistent with experimental findings in which OFC inactivation affects the ability to report confidence but not decision accuracy (Lak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model in light of experimental findings, supported by citation.

claim: The results support the actor-critic picture for reward-based learning, in which one circuit directly computes the policy while a second structure computes expected future reward to guide learning.
source: Our results thus support the actor-critic picture for reward-based learning, in which one circuit directly computes the policy to be followed, while a second structure, receiving projections from the decision network as well as information about the selected actions, computes expected future reward to guide learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of the actor-critic framework.

claim: Actor-critic models have a rich history in neuroscience, particularly in studies of the basal ganglia.
source: Actor-critic models have a rich history in neuroscience, particularly in studies of the basal ganglia (Houk et al., 1995; Dayan and Balleine, 2002; Joel et al., 2002; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Takahashi et al., 2008; Maia, 2010)
evidence: This is a statement about the history of actor-critic models in neuroscience, supported by citations.

claim: There is experimental evidence that signals in the striatum are more suitable for direct policy search rather than for updating action values as an intermediate step.
source: and it is interesting to note that there is some experimental evidence that signals in the striatum are more suitable for direct policy search rather than for updating action values as an intermediate step, as would be the case for purely value function-based approaches to computing the decision policy (Li and Daw, 2011; Niv and Langdon, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental evidence, supported by citations.

claim: The decision networks may correspond to circuits in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, while the value networks may correspond to circuits in OFC or basal ganglia.
source: Anatomically, the decision networks may correspond to circuits in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, while the value networks may correspond to circuits in OFC (Schultz et al., 2000; Takahashi et al., 2011) or basal ganglia (Hikosaka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the anatomical correspondence of the model components, supported by citations.

claim: The use of BPTT to compute gradients makes the plasticity rule not biologically plausible.
source: As in many other supervised learning approaches used previously to train RNNs (Mante et al., 2013; Song et al., 2016), the use of BPTT to compute the gradients (in particular, the eligibility) make our 'plasticity rule' not biologically plausible.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the approach, with citations to related work.

claim: It is somewhat surprising that the activity of networks trained with biologically implausible learning rules nevertheless exhibit many features found in neural activity recorded from behaving animals.
source: As noted previously (Zipser and Andersen, 1988), it is indeed somewhat surprising that the activity of the resulting networks nevertheless exhibit many features found in neural activity recorded from behaving animals.
evidence: This is an observation about the results, with citation to prior work.

claim: Recent work suggests that exact backpropagation is not necessary and can even be implemented in 'spiking' stochastic units.
source: Still, recent work suggests that exact backpropagation is not necessary and can even be implemented in 'spiking' stochastic units (Lillicrap et al., 2016), and that approximate forms of backpropagation and SGD can be implemented in a biologically plausible manner (Scellier and Bengio, 2016), including both spatially and temporally asynchronous updates in RNNs (Jaderberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about recent developments in biologically plausible learning, supported by citations.

claim: Miconi (2016) used a 'node perturbation'-based algorithm with an error signal at the end of each trial to train RNNs for several cognitive tasks.
source: Recently, Miconi (2016) used a 'node perturbation'-based (Fiete and Seung, 2006; Fiete et al., 2007; Hoerzer et al., 2014) algorithm with an error signal at the end of each trial to train RNNs for several cognitive tasks, and indeed, node perturbation is closely related to the REINFORCE algorithm used in this work.
evidence: This is a statement about related work, supported by citations.

claim: The method described in Miconi (2016) is more biologically plausible in the sense of not requiring gradients computed via backpropagation through time.
source: On one hand, the method described in Miconi (2016) is more biologically plausible in the sense of not requiring gradients computed via backpropagation through time as in our approach
evidence: This is a comparison to related work.

claim: In contrast to the networks in this work, those in Miconi (2016) did not 'commit' to a discrete action and thus the error signal was a graded quantity.
source: on the other hand, in contrast to the networks in this work, those in Miconi (2016) did not 'commit' to a discrete action and thus the error signal was a graded quantity.
evidence: This is a comparison to related work.

claim: In Miconi (2016) and other works, the prediction error was computed by algorithmically keeping track of a stimulus-specific running average of rewards.
source: In this and other works (Frémaux et al., 2010), moreover, the prediction error was computed by algorithmically keeping track of a stimulus (task condition)-specific running average of rewards.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in related work, supported by citations.

claim: The value network used in this work automatically depends on the stimulus, without requiring an external learning system to maintain a separate record for each trial type.
source: Here we used a concrete scheme (namely a value network) for approximating the average that automatically depends on the stimulus, without requiring an external learning system to maintain a separate record for each (true) trial type, which is not known by the agent with certainty.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the approach used in this work.

claim: Direct supervised learning can be mixed with reward-based learning using the REINFORCE algorithm by including only the eligibility term without modulating by reward.
source: One of the advantages of the REINFORCE algorithm for policy gradient reinforcement learning is that direct supervised learning can also be mixed with reward-based learning, by including only the eligibility term in Equation 3 without modulating by reward (Mnih et al., 2014), i.e., by maximizing the log-likelihood of the desired actions.
evidence: This is a statement about a feature of the REINFORCE algorithm, supported by citation.

claim: All of the networks in this work were trained from reward feedback only.
source: Although all of the networks in this work were trained from reward feedback only, it will be interesting to investigate this feature of the REINFORCE algorithm.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in the study.

claim: The REINFORCE algorithm allows for learning policies for continuous action spaces.
source: Another advantage, which we have not exploited here, is the possibility of learning policies for continuous action spaces (Peters and Schaal, 2008; Wierstra et al., 2009); this would allow us, for example, to model arbitrary saccade targets in the perceptual decision-making task, rather than limiting the network to discrete choices.
evidence: This is a statement about a feature of the REINFORCE algorithm, supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in the mammalian cortex have purely excitatory or inhibitory effects on other neurons, which is a consequence of Dale's Principle for neurotransmitters.
source: For instance, neurons in the mammalian cortex have purely excitatory or inhibitory effects on other neurons, which is a consequence of Dale's Principle for neurotransmitters (Eccles et al., 1954).
evidence: This is a statement about a biological constraint, supported by citation.

claim: The units used in this work are capable of dynamically modulating their time constants and gating their recurrent inputs.
source: In this work we did not include such constraints due to the more complex nature of our rectified GRUs (Equations 9–12); in particular, the units we used are capable of dynamically modulating their time constants and gating their recurrent inputs, and we therefore interpreted the firing rate units as a mixture of both excitatory and inhibitory populations.
evidence: This is a description of the model units used in the study.

claim: The units used in this work may implement the 'reservoir of time constants' observed experimentally.
source: Indeed, these may implement the 'reservoir of time constants' observed experimentally (Bernacchia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological interpretation of the model units, supported by citation.

claim: Methods for revealing neural mechanisms in trained RNNs remain limited to state-space analysis.
source: However, methods for revealing neural mechanisms in such networks remain limited to state-space analysis (Sussillo and Barak, 2013), which in particular does not reveal how the synaptic connectivity leads to the dynamics responsible for implementing the higher-level decision policy.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current analysis methods, with citation.

claim: General and systematic methods for analyzing trained networks are still needed and are the subject of ongoing investigation.
source: General and systematic methods for analyzing trained networks are still needed and are the subject of ongoing investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Reward-based training of RNNs makes it more likely that the resulting networks will correspond closely to biological networks observed in experiments with behaving animals.
source: Nevertheless, reward-based training of RNNs makes it more likely that the resulting networks will correspond closely to biological networks observed in experiments with behaving animals.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the approach.
